Enhanced heavy metal stability of sludge anaerobic digestion by different 
dosages of air nanobubble water
Tianfeng Wang a,*, Ziying Xu a, Jie Wang a, Siqi Ren a, Cheng Peng a, Dan Luo a, Xuemei Zhang b,  
Miaozhi Yang c
a College of Petrochemical Engineering, Lanzhou University of Technology, Lanzhou 730050, China
b College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Yan’an University, Yan’an 716000, China
c Yuzhong Zhongtie Environmental Protection Water Co., Ltd, Lanzhou 730101, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Editor: Wenshan Guo
Keywords:
Nanobubble water
Anaerobic digestion
Heavy metal speciation
Valence state
Potential ecological risks
A B S T R A C T
Nanobubbled water (NBW) can improve the performance of sludge anaerobic digestion (AD) to enhance 
digestate dewaterability. However, the effects of different doses of NBW on the stability of heavy metals (HMs) 
remain unknown. This study found that NBW increased the ultimate methane production of sludge AD by 11.7 
%–16.0 %. Compared with the corresponding control groups, the 40 % Air-NBW group (A40) presented the best 
improvement in methane production and digestate dewaterability of the three different dose groups (20 %, 40 %, 
and 60 % NBW: mixed substrates). NBW contributed to decreasing the proportion of HMs in the unstable 
exchangeable/acid-soluble fraction and promoting the conversion of heavy metal ions to stable low-valence 
states and low-energy levels. These low-valence states and low-energy levels of HMs were positively corre­
lated with digestate dewaterability and methane production. NBW reduced the potential ecological risk index 
(RI) of HMs by 4.2 %–42.0 %, with the A40 showing the greatest reduction in ecological risks. The RI of HMs was 
negatively correlated with methane production and digestate dewaterability. NBW can simultaneously improve 
methane production, digestate dewaterability, and heavy metal stability in sludge AD, with 40 % NBW being the 
optimal dose. This study provides a new sludge treatment strategy for controlling HMs pollution.
1. Introduction
The global production of sewage sludge is projected to reach 
approximately 130 million tons by 2030 (with a moisture content of 80 
%) [1]. As the final product of municipal sewage treatment plants, 
dewatered sludge (DS) is rich in biodegradable organic matter, 
including proteins, polysaccharides, and lignocellulose, which are ad­
vantageous for agricultural applications after treatment [2]. However, 
DS also contains certain heavy metals (HMs), which can significantly 
diminish its usability and pose serious risks to environmental and 
ecological security [3]. Anaerobic digestion (AD) has emerged as the 
predominant technology for treating DS [4]. This process not only 
generates clean energy and reduces sludge volume but also stabilizes 
HMs within the sludge to some extent [2,5]. Nevertheless, conventional 
AD still encounters several challenges, such as low methane production, 
poor dewaterability, and limited stabilization of HMs [6].
To improve sludge AD performance and enhance the stability of 
HMs, exogenous additives have been widely employed [6,7]. Nanoscale 
zero-valent iron used in the sludge mesophilic AD process increased 
cumulative methane production by 45.8 % and simultaneously 
increased the residual states of zinc (Zn) (from 15.1 % to 27.5 %) and 
nickel (Ni) (from 15.1 % to 26.0 %) [7]. Using biochar for sludge AD 
increased the oxidizable (from 23.0 % to 27.0 %) and residual (from 9.5 
% to 17.5 %) states of lead (Pb) [6]. However, these approaches may 
inadvertently contribute to secondary environmental pollution, thereby 
restricting the subsequent agricultural utilization of digestate [8]. In

addition, the improved dewaterability can reduce the toxicity and po­
tential risks of HMs in DS [9,10]. Consequently, an environmentally 
friendly and economically viable comprehensive strategy needs to be 
proposed to enhance the stabilization of HMs based on improved 
methane production performance and digestate dewaterability.
Nanobubble water (NBW) contains a substantial number of bubbles 
with diameters <1 μm [11]. Due to the high pressure, small diameter, 
and large specific surface area of nanobubbles, NBW exhibits properties 
not found in conventional water. These properties include high gas 
solubility, strong adsorption, extended storage time, and high zeta po­
tential [12]. The hydroxyl radicals generated upon the collapse of 
nanobubbles in Air-NBW are highly oxidizing and contribute to the 
decomposition of complex substrates, leading to a 19.1 % increase in 
methane production in the AD system [13]. Air-NBW can effectively 
alleviate ammonia inhibition by stimulating the activities of coenzyme 
F420 and hydrolase, resulting in a 12 %–39 % increase in methane pro­
duction [14]. Furthermore, the high surface activity of nanobubbles can 
alter the charge distribution on the surface of sludge particles, thereby 
enabling the release of bound water from improved flocs. Different types 
of NBW (Air, CO2, He, and N2) have been shown to reduce the specific 
resistance to filtration (SRF) and capillary suction time (CST) of diges­
tate by 18.8 %–29.6 % and 14.6 %–18.2 %, respectively [15]. However, 
the effects of different doses of NBW on methane production, digestate 
dewaterability, and the stability of HMs in sludge AD have been rarely 
investigated. In addition, the correlation between methane production, 
digestate dewaterability, and the stability of HMs remains unknown.
This study investigated the effects of different dosages of Air-NBW on 
methane production, microbial communities, and dewaterability of DS. 
The speciation and valence changes of HMs by Air-NBW were further 
explored, and the potential ecological risk index (RI) and the potential 
ecological risk factor of single metal (Er) were used to comprehensively 
assess the potential of Air-NBW to mitigate the ecological risks of HMs. 
Finally, the stability and ecological risks of HMs in sludge AD were 
analyzed in relation to methane production and digestate dewater­
ability. This study contributes to developing an efficient strategy for 
resource recovery while controlling HMs pollution.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
DS served as the substrate, which was obtained from a sewage 
treatment plant, employing an “oxidation ditch + biological aerated 
filter” process with a 6000 m3 d−1 treatment capacity. The seed sludge 
was taken from a mesophilic anaerobic digester in the laboratory. 
Table 1 shows the main parameters of different sludge.
2.2. Experimental process
The preparation of Air-NBW was consistent with Wang et al. [15], 
and the average particle size and concentration of nanobubbles were 
135.8 nm and 537 million mL−1 (Fig. S1). The anaerobic digesters were 
consistent with Xu et al. [4] (Fig. 1). DS was mixed with Air-NBW or 
deionized water in different mass ratios (water: DS = 2: 8, 4: 6, and 6: 4), 
and then they were mixed with seed sludge (10: 1), with a total amount 
of 1500 g. According to the mass ratios of Air-NBW or deionized water to 
the mixture of water and DS, which were 20 %, 40 %, and 60 %, the 
study was divided into six groups, labeled A20, C20, A40, C40, A60, and 
C60. Table 2 shows the total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS) and 
substrate-to-inoculum (S/I) ratio of the groups. Each group performed 
three parallel experiments with a total of 18 digesters. The water bath

temperature was 37 ± 2 ◦C, and the digestion period was 43 days.
2.3. Analytical methods
TS, VS, and pH of solid samples, soluble chemical oxygen demand 
(SCOD), and ammonia of liquid samples were measured using standard 
methods [16], and free ammonia nitrogen (FAN) of total ammonia ni­
trogen (TAN) was calculated using the specific calculation formula [17]. 
The gas chromatograph was used to determine the volatile fatty acid 
(VFA) of liquid samples (SP-7890Plus, Rui Hong, China), the acid gas 
flow meter was used to determine the biogas volume (LML-2, Alpha, 
China), and the biogas composition analyzer was used to determine the 
methane concentration (Biogas 5000, Geotech, UK). Methane produc­
tion was fitted using the modified Gompertz formula [13]. SRF mea­
surement methods were consistent with Yang et al. [18]. CST was 
measured with a capillary absorption meter (304 M, Triton Electronics, 
UK). The laser particle size analyzer was used to determine the digestate 
particle size (Nano ZS90, Malvern, UK).
The inductively coupled plasma emission mass spectrometer was 
used to quantify the concentration of HMs (ICP-MS 7850, Agilent, USA). 
The European Community Reference Bureau’s (BCR) sequential 
extraction procedure was used to determine the exchangeable/acid- 
soluble fraction (F1), the reducible fraction (F2), the oxidizable frac­
tion (F3), and the residual fraction (F4) of HMs. The F1 + F2 fractions 
are the bioavailability of HMs, expressed as the degree to which metal 
elements can interact with biological systems, and can be used to eval­
uate the toxicity of HMs [19]. The specific operation methods were 
consistent with Guo et al. [20]. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) 
was used to analyze the valence state of HMs (Escalab 250Xi, Thermo, 
USA). Finally, the Er and RI were calculated by the formulas to evaluate 
the environmental risks of HMs [21], in which the toxicity reaction 
factors (Tr) of copper (Cu), Ni, Zn, Pb, manganese (Mn), and chromium 
(Cr) were 5, 5, 1, 5, 1, and 2, respectively.
DNA was extracted from samples on day 8, and the high-throughput 
sequencing technology was used to analyze the microbial communities 
after adding different NBW. The V3-V4 portions of the bacterial 16S 
rRNA gene were amplified using primers 341F (5 ‘-CCTACGGGAGG­
CAGCAG-3’) and 806R (5 ‘-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3’); The V4- 
V5 portions of the archaeal 16S rRNA gene were amplified using 
primers Arch519F (5 ‘-CAGCCGCCGCGGTAA-3’) and Arch915R (5 
‘-GTGCTCCCCCGCCAATTCCT-3’). The sequencing data has been sub­
mitted online (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov). The accession numbers 
were PRJNA1236884 and PRJNA1236892. Prediction of genes from the 
sequencing data using PICRUSt2 to analyze the potential of key enzymes 
in microbial communities (https://github.com/picrust/picrust2). The 
kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes databases were used to 
analyze functional genes (https://www.kegg.jp/).
2.4. Statistical analysis
The statistical analysis was performed by SPSS (27.0) software. One- 
way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to test the differences 
between different experimental groups, and p < 0.05 means statistical 
significance. The correlation between the two parameters was analyzed 
by Spearman’s correlation coefficient, and * indicates p < 0.05, ** in­
dicates p < 0.01, and *** indicates p < 0.001. All data are expressed as 
mean ± standard deviation.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Digestion performance and microbial communities
On day 4, the VFA levels in the NBW groups increased by 10.5 %– 
20.3 % compared with the control (Fig. S2). NBW enhanced microbial 
activity and improved the hydrolysis performance of sludge AD [12]. On 
day 43, A20 and C20, which had higher solid content, exhibited VFA 
accumulation, potentially leading to acid inhibition and reduced 
methane production [22]. In this study, all groups showed high S/I ra­
tios (>10), with A20 and C20 exhibiting the highest values (Table 2). It 
was found that the increased S/I ratio would accelerate the rate of hy­
drolysis and acidification, enhance the formation of organic acid in­
termediates during AD, increase the risk of acid accumulation, and 
adversely affect methane production [23]. The pH, SCOD, TAN, and 
FAN are illustrated in Fig. S3. Compared with the control, the TAN in the 
NBW groups increased by 13.3 %–34.7 % (p < 0.01) on day 4. The 
collapse of nanobubbles releases chemical energy while generating hy­
droxyl radicals, which have strong oxidizing properties and contribute 
to the hydrolysis of proteins [24]. The rigid cell walls of microorganisms 
in sludge often reduce the efficiency of anaerobic degradation and 
prolong the hydraulic retention time, thereby affecting hydrolysis effi­
ciency [25]. Nanobubbles can create localized high pressure and 
microjets upon collapse that may destroy the cell walls of microorgan­
isms (e.g., peptidoglycan layers) [26]. In addition, the hydroxyl radicals 
generated by nanobubbles may oxidize lipids, proteins, and poly­
saccharides in the cell wall, destroying its integrity [12,27]. Once the 
cell wall is damaged, intracellular substances (e.g., proteins and poly­
saccharides) are released and further degraded, promoting hydrolysis 
and leading to increases in TAN and VFA [25]. This was confirmed by 
the elevation of VFA and TAN by the addition of NBW on day 4. In the 
later stage of AD, with the metabolism of VFA and the increase of TAN, 
the pH gradually showed an upward trend. The alkaline environment 
favors the growth of hydrogenotrophic methanogens [28]. The FAN of

the A20 and C20 exceeded 250 mg L−1 after day 23, so the methanogens 
may be subject to significant ammonia inhibition [29].
After day 8, all groups exhibited a general downward trend, and most 
of the organic matter in the A60 and C60 had been converted to methane 
(Fig. 2a). The decline observed in the other groups should be contributed 
by the ammonia inhibition of methanogen activity due to TAN greater 
than 1500 mg L−1 (Fig. S3) [4]. As the activity of methanogens gradually 
recovered, the methane production rate peaked on day 18. Among the 
control groups, the ultimate methane production of the C40 surpassed 
that of the others (Fig. 2b and Table S1). For the C20, high TS may have 
been influenced by FAN toxicity (Fig. S3), which could compromise the 
stability of the anaerobic system [14]. Furthermore, VFA accumulation 
might also lead to acid inhibition (Fig. S2) [22]. For the C60, when the 
TS was low, to meet the growth needs of microorganisms, some organic 
matter in the substrate was forced to synthesize new hydrolytic bacteria 
and methanogens, thus limiting methane production [30]. It was found 
that with the increase of sludge TS, methane production first increased 
and then decreased [30,31]. During sludge AD with different TS, the 
cumulative methane production in descending order was TS = 8 %, TS 
= 6 %, and TS = 12 % [32], which was similar to the trend observed in 
this study (Table 2). NBW significantly enhanced the methane produc­
tion by 14.1 % (p < 0.001), 16.0 % (p < 0.001), and 11.7 % (p < 0.05) for 
the A20, A40, and A60, respectively, compared with their corresponding 
controls. NBW promotes enzyme activity and increases electron transfer 
to stimulate the activity of methanogens, thus improving methane pro­
duction [12]. The lower content of nanobubbles in the A20 resulted in a 
weaker promoting effect compared with A40. Furthermore, since the 
control group had the optimal hydrolysis conditions, it limited the 
improvement efficiency of NBW on hydrolysis performance in the A60, 
consequently making the promoting effect of methane production less 
than that of the A40 [15].
At the phylum level, Bacteroidota (21.0 %–27.2 %), Proteobacteria 
(16.6 %–23.8 %), Firmicutes (13.4 %–22.2 %), Chloroflexi (8.0 %–10.2 
%), and Acidobacteriota (6.0 %–10.4 %) dominated the bacterial 
community (Fig. 3a). Bacteroidota and Firmicutes are known to partici­
pate in the hydrolysis of lignocellulose to generate short-chain fatty 
acids [4]. Compared with the control, the relative abundance of Bac­
teroidota and Firmicutes increased in the NBW groups. In addition, high 
S/I conditions can promote the activity of hydrolytic and acidogenic 
bacteria, thereby enhancing the hydrolysis performance [23]. In this 
study, the relative abundance of Bacteroidota and Firmicutes increased 
with increasing S/I ratios. At the genus level, Methanobacterium (64.0 %– 
76.6 %), Methanobrevibacter (11.8 %–26.4 %), and Methanomassiliicoccus 
(0.6 %–6.1 %) dominated the archaeal community (Fig. 3b). These 
genera are all hydrogenotrophic methanogens [15]. Hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens demonstrate strong tolerance under high ammonia, which 
has certain advantages in maintaining the methane production rate 
[33]. High S/I conditions can increase the activity of hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens, thereby promoting methane production [34]. Therefore, 
the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway was dominant in this 
study. The relative abundances of Methanobacterium and Methano­
brevibacter in the NBW groups were reduced by 0.1 %–2.6 % and 0.6 %– 
3.2 %, respectively, compared with the control. This reduction suggests 
a shift in the archaeal community structure, indicating that more types 
of methanogens were involved in the methanogenesis process. This 
implies that NBW stimulated the activity of more types of archaea, 
which is beneficial to the increase in the diversity of the archaea com­
munity and makes methanogenesis metabolism active [35]. The abun­
dance changes of key enzymes in major methanogenesis pathways are 
presented in Fig. S4. The abundance of key enzymes involved in the 
M00567 pathway was increased in the NBW groups, compared with the 
control. NBW made hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis metabolism 
more active.
3.2. Dewaterability
Particle size (d50) is an important factor affecting digestate dew­
aterability [36]. Smaller particles possess a larger specific surface area,

facilitating the separation of water [37]. Lower TS levels enhance mass 
transfer efficiency and promote a more complete degradation of organic 
matter within the sludge [30]. However, the d50 of C60 exceeded that of 
C40 (Fig. 4a). This may be because small particles of sludge are more 
readily utilized, while large particles of sludge tend to remain under low 
organic loading conditions, thereby increasing the average particle size 
of digestate after AD [4]. The d50 of the A20, A40, and A60 decreased by 
3.4 %, 20.1 % (p < 0.001), and 9.7 % (p < 0.01), respectively, compared 
with their corresponding controls. Nanobubbles enhanced the mass 
transfer efficiency, improved the hydrolysis performance, and decreased 
the particle size of digestate, thereby enhancing the dewaterability 
[15,38]. Among the NBW groups, A40 exhibited the best improvement 
in hydrolysis performance. The TAN improved by 4.1 %, 7.5 %, and 5.2 
% for A20, A40, and A60, respectively, compared with the control on 
day 43 (Fig. S3). Consequently, A40 demonstrated the most pronounced 
reduction in d50.
Zeta potential is the crucial index to evaluate the surface electro­
negativity of digestate [36]. With the increase in zeta potential, the 
collision of digestate particles is promoted, leading to the release of 
bound water from the improved digestate flocs and enhancing digestate 
dewaterability [15]. Lower TS improves the degradation of digestate 
flocs and reduces electrostatic repulsion between particles, resulting in 
increased zeta potential (Fig. 4b) [39]. The Zeta potential of the A20, 
A40, and A60 increased by 6.9 % (p < 0.01), 9.2 % (p < 0.01), and 8.5 % 
(p < 0.01), respectively, compared with the control. Nanobubbles can 
attract and immobilize cations in the digestate through electrostatic 
interaction to neutralize the negative charges on the surface of digestate 
particles, thereby reducing electrostatic repulsion on the surface and 
increasing the zeta potential [40]. Although lower TS generally leads to 
more complete organic matter degradation, A40 exhibited the most 
significant increase in zeta potential among the NBW groups. This may 
be because a higher dosage of NBW can lead to excessive aggregation of 
nanobubbles within the digestate, potentially disrupting the floc struc­
ture and consequently increasing the electrostatic repulsion of the flocs 
to some extent [12,39]. Therefore, an appropriate dosage of NBW is 
more conducive to enhancing dewaterability.
SRF can reflect the consistency and structural characteristics of 
sludge, and lower SRF values are favorable for microbial infiltration and 
degradation [41]. CST refers to the time required to measure the 
permeation distance of moisture in sludge on filter paper under specific 
conditions [41]. Digestate particle size and Zeta potential can indirectly 
reflect the changes in SRF and CST by affecting flocs’ structure and 
porosity. Organic matter degradation in AD led to a decrease in the 
particle size of digestate and reduced the electrostatic repulsion between 
particles, which facilitates the aggregation of digestate particles into 
larger flocs, increasing the porosity of digestate, thus leading to the 
enhancement of digestate permeability [39,42]. The SRF of the A20, 
A40, and A60 decreased by 2.2 %, 29.8 % (p < 0.05), and 23.1 % (p <
0.05), respectively, compared with the control (Fig. 4c). The CST of the 
A20, A40, and A60 decreased by 1.9 %, 13.4 % (p < 0.001), and 11.8 %, 
respectively, compared with the control (Fig. 4d). The most significant 
reduction of SRF and CST was observed in A40, aligning with the results 
of digestate particle size and Zeta potential. Due to its high permeability, 
NBW can enter into the interior of digestate particles and degrade the 
extracellular polymers to release bound water by using active substances 
released when the nanobubbles collapsed; meanwhile, under the action 
of the nanobubbles, the charges on the surface of particles were partially 
neutralized and the electrostatic repulsion between particles was

3.3. Speciation distribution of heavy metals
HMs are immobilized in sludge through various chemical and bio­
logical interactions, exhibiting non-degradability and certain toxicity 
[44]. Therefore, it is essential to mitigate the potential ecological risks 
by transforming HMs to a stable state [45]. According to the distribution 
of HMs in municipal sludge across various regions of China [46], it can 
be seen that compared with other HMs, the contents of cadmium, mer­
cury, and arsenic in municipal sludge were extremely low. In the 
western region where this study was conducted, cadmium and arsenic 
were not major pollutants. In comparison, Cu, Ni, Zn, Pb, Mn, and Cr 
have greater research value in the municipal sludge of western China.

The HMs speciation stability increases in the order of F1, F2, F3, and F4, 
with the F1 fraction being the most readily available to organisms [20].
Overall, the F1 fraction of each metal decreased after AD. The F1 
fractions of Cu, Ni, Zn, Pb, Mn, and Cr were reduced to 0.9 %–1.3 %, 
27.8 %–35.3 %, 18.4 %–20.4 %, 0.6 %–4.5 %, 22.4 %–22.7 %, and 0.1 
%–0.1 %, respectively (Fig. 5). Generally, changes in environmental 
factors can directly influence the stability of HMs. The moderate in­
crease in pH is beneficial to the stabilization of HMs [45]. During AD, the 
consumption of VFA and the increase of ammonia nitrogen indirectly 
promoted the stabilization of HMs by raising pH (Figs. S2–3). In addi­
tion, the bioavailability fractions (F1 + F2) of Cu, Ni, Zn, Pb, and Mn 
were reduced. The bioavailability fraction of Cr showed an increase, 
possibly due to the release of chlorine into metal halide formation, 
which converted poorly soluble metal complexes into soluble metal 
chlorides (e.g., CrCl3) [47]. Cr is considered one of the least bioavailable 
metals [45], and the initial amount of Cr was minimal compared with 
other HMs, so the change in its bioavailability had little impact on 
ecological risks. The F4 fraction of Cu, Ni, Pb, and Mn all increased, 
while the F4 fraction of Zn slightly decreased (except for the A40). This 
may be because, in addition to complexing with organic functional 
groups, Zn also tends to react with sulfides to produce ZnS precipitates 
[48]. The ZnS precipitates are readily soluble under strongly oxidizing 
and strongly acidic conditions, so in the final step of BCR, Zn remained 
in the supernatant after the precipitate was dissolved, resulting in an 
increase in its F3 fraction [20]. In summary, AD positively impacted the 
stabilization of HMs (Table S2).
NBW affected the formal transformation of HMs, primarily reflected 
in the changes observed in each fraction of HMs. After AD, the F1 
fraction of each metal in the NBW groups was reduced compared with 
the control. The F1 fraction of Cu, Ni, Zn, Pb, Mn, and Cr decreased by 
0.2 %–0.8 %, 1.8 %–6.4 %, 1.1 %–3.8 %, 0.3 %–3.8 %, 2.9 %–4.6 %, and 
0.0 %–0.1 %, respectively (subtraction of percentages). NBW possesses a 
high specific surface area and strong adsorption force, which may enable 
it to adsorb heavy metal ions (HMI) in digestate efficiently [12]. 
Compared with the control, the F4 fraction of each metal in the NBW 
groups was increased. The F4 fraction of Cu, Ni, Zn, Pb, Mn, and Cr 
increased by 0.0 %–2.0 %, 0.3 %–11.2 %, 0.4 %–4.1 %, 1.4 %–5.1 %, 8.7 
%–11.1 %, and 2.0 %–5.0 %, respectively (subtraction of percentages). 
Nanobubbles are capable of enhancing the hydrolysis of complex 
organic matter. The products of this process (e.g., humic acid) contain 
abundant functional groups that can form stable complexes with HMI 
[45,49]. All the above results indicate that NBW is beneficial in con­
verting HMs into a more stable form, thereby mitigating the ecotoxicity 
and risks of HMs, which provides convenience for subsequent digestate 
disposal.
Different proportions of NBW exhibited varying effects on the sta­
bilization of HMs. Among all groups with NBW, only the bioavailability 
fraction (F1 + F2) of each metal in the A40 was reduced compared with 
the control. Compared with other proportions of groups with NBW, A40 
was more conducive to stabilizing HMs. Meanwhile, the enhancement 
rate of the F4 fraction for each metal in the A40 surpassed that in the 
other groups with NBW. Notably, this is consistent with the conclusion 
of protein hydrolysis in AD systems. The increasing concentration of 
TAN was the most significant in the A40, exceeding that seen in the A20 
and A60, compared with the control (Fig. S3). NBW may have stimu­
lated the activity of microorganisms, enabling extracellular polymers 
produced through their metabolism to interact with HMI present in 
digestate, facilitating the stabilization of the HMI complex [11,50].
3.4. Risk assessment of heavy metals
Er and RI have been widely used to evaluate the HMs’ potential 
ecological risks in sludge substrates [21]. Generally, RI is categorized 
into four levels: low risk (RI < 50), medium risk (50 < RI 〈100), 
considerable risk (100 < RI 〈200), and high risk (RI > 200) [51]. Prior to 
AD, the RI of HMs in sludge was observed to be approximately 330, 
indicating a very high risk to the ecosystem (Fig. 6a). After AD, the 
ecological risks of each group were effectively reduced, and the RI 
remained around 260. Notably, the RI of the NBW groups was 4.2 %– 
42.0 % lower than that of the control, demonstrating that the potential 
environmental harm of HMs could be effectively reduced by NBW 
treatment. The RI of A40 and A60 fell below the threshold of 200. 
Among them, A40 exhibited the lowest ecological risk, which was 
reduced by 54.2 % compared with the RI of sludge before AD. Duncan’s

for the high Er of Cu.
3.5. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy analysis
XPS can be used to analyze the chemical composition of samples and 
determine the valence state of elements [52]. The characteristic peaks of 
the binding energy of HMs can be used to identify the element species, 
and the shifts of binding energy reflect the change in the valence state of 
HMs [53].
According to the XPS results, the proportion of more toxic high- 
valence HMI was greater than that of low-valence HMI before AD 
(Figs. S5–10). The proportion of low-valence HMI gradually increased 
with the progression of AD. The proportion of Cu+ increased from 31.2 
% to 55.9 %–73.0 %, and Cu2+ gradually converted to Cu+ (Fig. 7). Cu2+
usually exists in combination with organic matter, while Cu+ usually 
exists in combination with sulfur [54]. After AD, most of the organic 
matter was consumed, gradually decreasing the proportion of Cu2+. Mn 
and Cr also exhibited the same pattern. The proportion of Mn2+
increased from 28.6 % to 32.0 %–35.2 %, and Mn4+ eventually changed 
to Mn2+ through Mn3+ transition. The proportion of Cr3+ increased from 
31.5 % to 60.4 %–65.3 %, and Cr6+ gradually changed to Cr3+. These 
findings indicate that AD can promote the occurrence of the reduction 
reaction of HMs, which gradually transforms the high-valence HMI into 
the low-valence state. This was further evidenced by the significant 
correlation of the altered valence states of Cu and Mn with their 
reducible state fraction (F2). The hydrogenotrophic methanogen Meth­
anobacterium may promote the reduction of HMs, making them more 
stable [55,56]. Methanobacterium dominated the methanogenesis pro­
cess (Fig. 3) and benefited the reduction and stabilization of HMs. 
Moreover, with the progress of AD, HMs gradually transformed from 
high energy levels to stable low energy levels. Ni2+ and Zn2+ gradually 
converted from 2p3/2 to 2p1/2, and Pb2+ gradually converted from 4f7/2 
to 4f5/2. The proportions of Ni2+2p1/2, Zn2+2p1/2, and Pb2+4f5/2 
increased from initial 49.7 %, 10.9 % and 3.5 % to 52.0 %–59.2 %, 19.2 
%–45.7 %, and 8.7 %–41.9 %, respectively. Through the conversion of 
the valence state and energy level of HMI, it can be seen that AD can 
promote HMs to exist in digestate in a more stable and less toxic form.

portions of Cu+, Mn2+, and Cr3+ increased by 11.8 %–23.1 %, 10.4 %–

The proportions of Ni2+2p1/2, Zn2+2p1/2, and Pb2+4f5/2 increased by 
4.7 %–8.7 %, 4.6 %–77.7 %, and 5.1 %–56.1 % after adding NBW, 
respectively (subtraction of percentages). All the above results indicate 
that NBW can promote the conversion of HMI in digestate to a stable 
valence state and energy level, making it more prone to complexation 
and precipitation. The local high-energy environment generated by 
nanobubbles during the collapse process can promote the reduction of 
HMI and the change of energy state, so NBW can function as a reducing 
agent to transform HMs into more stable and less soluble speciation 
[57,58].
Nanobubbles possess strong mobility and can transfer HMs to the 
surface of sludge particles [59]. Part of the negative charges on the 
surface of sludge particles were neutralized, increasing the Zeta poten­
tial, and the HMI gradually transformed from high-valence to low- 
valence states. Among all NBW groups, the proportions of Mn2+, Cr3+, 
Ni2+2p1/2, Zn2+2p1/2, and Pb2+4f5/2 increased the most in the A40. This 
is consistent with the conclusion that the A40 experienced the greatest 
enhancement in Zeta potential (Fig. 4b). Therefore, it can be speculated 
that there exists a correlation between the dewaterability and the sta­
bilization of HMs of sludge AD. After the analysis, the HMI of all low 
valence states and low energy levels were negatively correlated with 
digestate particle size, SRF, and CST, while positively correlated with 
Zeta potential (Fig. 8). The HMI of all high valence states and high en­
ergy levels were positively correlated with digestate particle size, SRF, 
and CST, while negatively correlated with Zeta potential. Furthermore, 
Zn2+2p1/2 and Mn2+ reached the highest proportional values in the A40, 
96.9 % and 89.6 %, respectively. This may be because the initial content 
of Zn and Mn was significantly higher than that of other HMs (Fig. 5), 
which was more conducive to the changes in the valence states by NBW. 
Correlation analysis observed that HMs with larger initial content were 
more significantly correlated with the changes in valence states.
Notably, methane production was positively correlated with the HMI 
of low valence states and low energy levels, while negatively correlated 
with the HMI of high valence states and high energy levels (Fig. 8). 
Improved methanogenesis performance was beneficial to stabilizing 
HMs. Further analysis revealed that the RI of HMs was significantly 
positively correlated with SRF and CST (p < 0.05), while negatively 
correlated with methane production (Fig. 9). Therefore, NBW may affect 
the stability of HMs and the potential ecological risks by changing 
methanogenesis and dewaterability.
3.6. Application analysis
NBW is becoming a hot spot in the field of AD, with commonly uti­
lized gas types including CO2, O2, Air, N2, and H2 [12]. Among these 
options, the raw materials of Air-NBW are cost-free and have high 
economic value. The preparation method for Air-NBW is straightfor­
ward. Only a single instrument is needed to pump air into water, and the 
labor cost is low. By enhancing hydrolysis and stimulating the activity of 
methanogens, NBW can not only achieve a higher level of methane 
production and a more stable AD system but also improve the structure 
of flocs and significantly improve the dewaterability of digestate. 
Consequently, in engineering applications, the addition of NBW can 
reduce the dosage of flocculants needed after AD. In addition, the pre­
pared Air-NBW is colorless and non-toxic and will not cause pollution 
during application, so it will not pose a threat to the environment [38]. 
Most importantly, Air-NBW promoted the conversion of HMs form

4. Conclusions
Among the three different dose groups, the 40 % NBW group (A40) 
exhibited the best methanogenesis and dewaterability of the final 
digestate, with a 16.0 % increase in methane production and a 29.8 % 
and 13.4 % decrease in SRF and CST, respectively, compared with the 
control. Additionally, NBW favored decreasing the proportion of HMs 
with the unstable exchangeable/acid-soluble fraction and promoted the 
conversion of HMI to stable low-valence states and low-energy levels in 
the digestate. The low-valence states and low-energy levels of HMs were 
positively correlated with digestate dewaterability and methane pro­
duction. NBW effectively reduced the potential ecological risks of HMs, 
as evidenced by a 42.0 % decrease in the RI of A40 compared with the 
control. The RI was significantly positively correlated with SRF and CST, 
while negatively correlated with methane production. This study pro­
vides a novel sludge treatment strategy for controlling the pollution of 
HMs and efficient land use.
